title: Relationship quality varies across cultures and life situations, with age, religious participation, partnership status, and employment shaping social well-being differently across countries
source_unit: Wilkinson et al., Strangers, Friends, and Everything Between: Sociodemographic Variation in Social Relationship Quality Across 22 Countries, Social Indicators Research 2026
geography: 22 countries in Wave 1 of the Global Flourishing Study, including non-Western and Western national contexts

observations.period: Global Flourishing Study Wave 1; cross-national social relationship quality

denominator.unit: adults in nationally representative samples across 22 countries

relationship_quality_scale.value: global subjective relationship-quality score based on contentment with friendships and relationships and satisfaction with relationships, measured 0-10

country_range.value: country averages were mostly between 7 and 8, with observed high-low difference of 8.68 versus 5.96

higher_average_contexts.value: Indonesia, the Philippines, and Mexico showed higher average relationship-quality scores, while Japan, Turkey, and Australia showed lower averages

cultural_variation.value: country differences did not reduce to a simple individualism-collectivism rule; important exceptions and within-country variation remained

observations.method: Nationally representative Wave 1 Global Flourishing Study samples with post-stratification and nonresponse adjustments; country-specific estimates were combined using random-effects meta-analysis and analyzed across sociodemographic groups.
observations.uncertainty: The measure is subjective and broad, cross-cultural translation and response-style differences may affect country comparisons, and the 22-country sample should not be generalized to countries outside the study.
observations.subgroup: Adults across 22 countries, with variation by age, religious-service attendance, marital status, employment, gender, education, and immigration status.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher scores may reflect cultural response styles, expectations, relationship norms, or sample composition rather than objectively stronger social networks or universally better social conditions.

observations.period: Global Flourishing Study Wave 1; age and religious participation

age_pattern.value: older adults reported higher social relationship quality on average, with the pattern relatively consistent across countries

religious_service_pattern.value: more frequent religious-service attendance was associated with higher relationship quality across countries

community_route.value: religious participation may provide repeated opportunities for shared values, social contact, care, and relationship maintenance

life_course_route.value: age-related selectivity and investment in close, meaningful relationships may help explain higher reported quality among older adults

observations.method: Country-specific analyses and pooled random-effects meta-analysis of relationship-quality scores by age and religious-service attendance.
observations.uncertainty: The data are cross-sectional and do not establish that religious attendance or age causes better relationships; health, selection, community access, cultural norms, and survivorship may contribute.
observations.subgroup: Older and younger adults, and adults with different frequencies of religious-service attendance across the 22 countries.
observations.counterinterpretation: People with stronger relationships or better health may be more able and willing to attend religious services; religious participation can also exclude or burden some groups.

observations.period: Global Flourishing Study Wave 1; partnership and employment status

partnership_pattern.value: married and widowed adults reported higher relationship quality than separated and divorced adults

employment_pattern.value: retired adults reported the highest relationship quality and unemployed adults the lowest

work_social_route.value: unemployment may reduce relationship quality through stigma, withdrawal, job-search strain, or shared causes such as depression or addiction

country_variation.value: patterns varied across nations, showing that marital and employment categories do not carry identical social meaning everywhere

observations.method: Country-specific nationally representative analyses and pooled meta-analytic comparisons by marital and employment status.
observations.uncertainty: The study cannot distinguish causal pathways between employment, partnership, health, and relationship quality; categories such as widowed, retired, unemployed, and separated contain heterogeneous life situations.
observations.subgroup: Married, widowed, separated, divorced, unemployed, employed, and retired adults across diverse national contexts.
observations.counterinterpretation: Relationship quality may influence employment and partnership stability as much as those statuses influence relationship quality; cultural and welfare-state differences may alter the meaning of each category.

observations.period: Global Flourishing Study Wave 1; implications for social infrastructure and policy

denominator.unit: countries in the study's cross-national comparison

social_resource.value: relationship quality is treated as a social resource associated with health and well-being across the life course

targeting_route.value: social-connection strategies should be tailored to national and sociodemographic distributions rather than assuming one universal intervention

community_infrastructure.value: employment settings, family and partnership systems, religious communities, and other repeated social institutions may shape access to meaningful relationships

measurement_boundary.value: global relationship quality is distinct from network size, contact frequency, social support, loneliness, and the quality of a specific relationship

observations.method: Authors' cross-national synthesis of descriptive and meta-analytic findings from the Global Flourishing Study.
observations.uncertainty: The study does not evaluate interventions, establish causal effects on health, or measure the institutional mechanisms that generate relationship quality; policy implications remain hypotheses for future research.
observations.subgroup: Policymakers, community organizations, employers, religious institutions, families, and adults in different life-course and socioeconomic positions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Formal institutions can provide connection but can also reproduce exclusion, stigma, coercion, or unequal access; higher reported relationship quality should not be equated with social equality.

related_sources.claim: Peer-reviewed open-access Social Indicators Research article using 202,898 adults in 22 countries from the Global Flourishing Study.
Publisher article page with abstract, methods, cross-national findings, sociodemographic results, discussion, and limitations.

boundary: This record adds a global relationship-quality route from culture and life situation through age, religious participation, partnership, employment, social resources, and targeted social infrastructure. It is cross-sectional subjective survey evidence with country-comparative and meta-analytic estimates, not longitudinal causal evidence, an objective social-network measure, or a universal cultural typology.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Publisher article and indexed full-text source reviewed for sample size, measure construction, country patterns, age and religious-attendance associations, marital and employment differences, cross-national exceptions, and methodological limitations.
